## Appendix A Omitted Proofs From Section 3.1

### A.1 Global Minimizers of The Sigmoid Loss are $(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})$ -Constellations

We will repeatedly use the following fact which follows from $\log(1+\exp(\kappa))\geq 0$ for any $\kappa\in\mathbb{R}.$

#### Observation 3.

For any $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and $t,b,$ it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\max\Bigg(\max_{i}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+b)\Big),\max_{i\neq j}\log\Big(1+\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-b)\Big)\Bigg) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\leq\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t,b) \displaystyle\leq N^{2}\times\max\Bigg(\max_{i}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+b)\Big),\max_{i\neq j}\log\Big(1+\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-b)\Big)\Bigg). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Suppose that $\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t^{(s)},b^{(s)})=0$ indeed holds. By, (13), this means that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t^{(s)}\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle+b^{(s)})\Big)=0\;\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\log\Big(1+\exp(t^{(s)}\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-b^{(s)})\Big)=0\;\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

Equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}-t^{(s)}\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle+b^{(s)}=-\infty\;\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}t^{(s)}\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-b^{(s)}=-\infty\;\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

Equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}t^{(s)}\Big(\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle-\frac{b^{(s)}}{t^{(s)}}\Big)=+\infty\;\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}t^{(s)}\Big(\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\frac{b^{(s)}}{t^{(s)}}\Big)=-\infty\;\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

In particular, as $t^{(s)}>0$ always, this means that for all large enough $s,$ the quantity $\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)}\coloneqq\frac{b^{(s)}}{t^{(s)}}$ satisfies that

$$ \displaystyle\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)} \displaystyle\geq 0\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)} \displaystyle\leq 0\qquad\forall i\neq j\,. $$

However, as all $U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}$ are unit vectors, $\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle\leq 1,\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle\geq-1$ holds for any $i,j,s.$ Hence, for all large enough $s,$ (15) and (16) imply that

$$ -1\leq\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)}\leq 1. $$

Now, observe that $\{U_{1}^{(s)},U_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,U_{N}^{(s)},V_{1}^{(s)},V_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,V_{N}^{(s)},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)}\}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{\otimes 2N}\times[-1,1].$ As $(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{\otimes 2N}\times[-1,1]$ is a compact set, $\{U_{1}^{(s)},U_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,U_{N}^{(s)},V_{1}^{(s)},V_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,V_{N}^{(s)},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^{+\infty}$ has a convergent subsequence. Suppose that it converges to $\{U_{1},U_{2},\ldots,U_{N},V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{N},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}\}.$ By (15) and (16), we have that

$$ \displaystyle\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}\geq 0\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}\leq 0\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

Setting

$$ \mathsf{m}=\min\Bigg(\min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}},\min_{i\neq j}\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}-\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\Bigg) $$

gives the desired result. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ are a $(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})$ -Constellation with some $\mathsf{m}>0.$ Then, for any $t,$ it holds that

$$ \displaystyle t(\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})\geq\mathsf{m}\times t\qquad\forall i, \displaystyle t(\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})\leq-\mathsf{m}\times t\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

In particular, by Observation (14), it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t,t\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}) \displaystyle\leq N^{2}\times\log\Big(1+\exp(-\mathsf{m}\times t)\Big) \displaystyle\leq N^{2}\exp(-\mathsf{m}\times t)=\exp(-\mathsf{m}\times t+2\log N/t)=\exp(-\mathsf{m}\times t+o(t)) $$

which proves the convergence to zero. Choosing $(\mathsf{m}^{*},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{*})$ in this argument, where

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{m}^{*}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}(\min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\max_{i\neq j}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle)>\frac{1}{2}((\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})-(-\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}))=\mathsf{m}>0, \displaystyle\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}^{*}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}(\min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+\max_{i\neq j}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle), $$

also proves that $\inf_{b}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t,b)\leq e^{-t\mathsf{m}^{*}+o(t)}.$

All that is left to show is that

$$ \inf_{b}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t,b)\geq e^{-t\mathsf{m}^{*}+o(t)}. $$

Equivalently, we can show that $\inf_{b}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Sig}}(\{U_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t,b)\geq\log\Big(1+e^{-t\mathsf{m}^{*}+o(t)}\Big)$ since $\log(1+\gamma)=\gamma+o(\gamma)$ as $\gamma\longrightarrow 0.$ However, by (13), for the last inequality, it is enough to show that

$$ \max\Bigg(\max_{i}\Big(-t\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+b)\Big),\max_{i\neq j}\Big(t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-b\Big)\Bigg)\geq-t\times\mathsf{m}^{*}\,. $$

Equivalently

$$ \min\Bigg(\min_{i}\Big(\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\frac{b}{t})\Big),\min_{i\neq j}\Big(-t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle+\frac{b}{t}\Big)\Bigg)\leq\mathsf{m}^{*}\,. $$

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that for some $b,t,$ we have that

$$ \min\Bigg(\min_{i}\Big(\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\frac{b}{t})\Big),\min_{i\neq j}\Big(-t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle+\frac{b}{t}\Big)\Bigg)=\mathsf{m}^{\prime}>\mathsf{m}^{*}. $$

Then,

$$ \min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\max_{i\neq j}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\frac{b}{t}+\mathsf{m}^{\prime}-(\frac{b}{t}-\mathsf{m}^{\prime})=2\mathsf{m}^{\prime}>2\mathsf{m}^{*}, $$

which is a contradiction with the definition of $\mathsf{m}^{*}.$ ∎

### A.2 Robustness of Nearest-Neighbor Retrieval: Proof of Proposition 1

Suppose that

$$ \displaystyle\expect_{(a_{j})_{j=1}^{B}\sim[N]^{\times k}}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{B}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{a_{j}},V_{a_{j}}\rangle+b)\Big) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\sum_{i\neq j}\log\Big(1+\exp(t\langle U_{a_{i}},V_{a_{j}}\rangle-b)\Big)\Big]\leq\xi\log 2. $$

holds. Again,as the function $x\longrightarrow\log(1+e^{x})$ is non-negative, this implies that for some $0\leq x\leq\xi,$

$$ \displaystyle x\log 2=\expect_{(a_{j})_{j=1}^{B}\sim[N]^{\times k}}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{B}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{a_{j}},V_{a_{j}}\rangle+b)\Big)\Big] \displaystyle=B\times\expect_{j\sim\textsf{unif}([N])}\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle+b)\Big). $$

However, whenever $t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle-b\leq 0,$ then $\log\Big(1+\exp(-t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle+b)\Big)\geq\log 2.$ By Markov’s inequality, it follows that

$$ \prob_{j\sim\textsf{unif}([N])}[t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle-b\leq 0]\leq\frac{x}{B}. $$

Hence, for all but at most a $\frac{x}{B}$ fraction of the data indices $j,$ it follows that $\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle>b/t.$

In the exact same way, for some $y\geq 0$ such that $x+y\leq\xi.$ it follows that

$$ \prob_{i,j\sim[N]^{\times 2}}[t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle-b\geq 0]\leq\frac{y}{B(B-1)}. $$

Note that for every fixed $i,$ if $\prob_{j\sim\textsf{unif}([N])|_{j\neq i}}[t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle-b>0]>0,$ then $\prob_{j\sim\textsf{unif}([N])|_{j\neq i}}[t\langle U_{j},V_{j}\rangle-b>0]\geq 1/(N-1).$ Hence, one can similarly argue that for all but at most a $\frac{y(N-1)}{B(B-1)}$ fraction of the data indices $i,$ it follows that $\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle<b/t$ for all $j.$ Thus, for at least a

$$ 1-\frac{x}{B}-\frac{y(N-1)}{B(B-1)} $$

fraction of the indices $i,$ it follows that for any $j\neq i,$

$$ \langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle>b/t>\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle. $$

Clearly, for these indices, nearest neighbor search succeeds. Optimizing over $0\leq x,0\leq y,x+y\leq\xi,$ we reach the conclusion.

### A.3 Global Minimizers of InfoNCE Loss

We claim that the following four results hold. Since the proofs are nearly identical to the ones for SigLIP, we only give one prove the third result.

#### Theorem A.1 (Necessary Condition for InfoNCE Global Minimizers).

Suppose that any iterative algorithm produces a sequence $\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},t^{(s)}>0$ for $s=1,2,\ldots$ such that

$$ \lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{InfoNCE}}(\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t^{(s)})=0. $$

Then, there exists some subsequence indexed by $(s_{r})_{r=1}^{+\infty}$ such that

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{r\longrightarrow+\infty}U_{i}^{(s_{r})}=U_{i},\quad\lim_{r\longrightarrow+\infty}V_{i}^{(s_{r})}=V_{i}\text{ for all }i\end{split} $$

and there exists some $\mathsf{m}\geq 0$ and $\{\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ such that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N},\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}$ satisfy:

$$ \begin{split}&\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle\geq\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)+m\qquad\forall i,\\
&\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\leq\min(\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i),\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(j))-m\qquad\forall i\neq j.\\
\end{split} $$

#### Theorem A.2 (Sufficient Condition for InfoNCE Global Minimizers).

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ satisfies (22) for some $\mathsf{m}>0$ and $\{\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)\}_{i=1}^{N}.$ Then,

$$ \lim_{t\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=0\,. $$

Moreover, for $\mathsf{m}^{*}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}(\min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\max_{i\neq j}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle),$

$$ \inf_{b}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=e^{-t\mathsf{m}^{*}+o(t)}. $$

For the other two results, consider the one-sided InfoNCE defined by

$$ \mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle)}{\sum_{j}\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle)}. $$

#### Theorem A.3 (Necessary Condition for one-sided InfoNCE Global Minimizers).

Suppose that any iterative algorithm produces a sequence $\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},t^{(s)}>0$ for $s=1,2,\ldots$ such that

$$ \lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t^{(s)})=0. $$

Then, there exists some subsequence indexed by $(s_{r})_{r=1}^{+\infty}$ such that

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{r\longrightarrow+\infty}U_{i}^{(s_{r})}=U_{i},\quad\lim_{r\longrightarrow+\infty}V_{i}^{(s_{r})}=V_{i}\text{ for all }i\end{split} $$

and there exists some $\mathsf{m}\geq 0$ and $\{\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ such that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N},\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}$ satisfy (3):

$$ \begin{split}&\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle\geq\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)+m\qquad\forall i,\\
&\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\leq\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)-m\qquad\forall i\neq j.\\
\end{split} $$

#### Theorem A.4 (Sufficient Condition for one-sided InfoNCE Global Minimizers).

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ satisfies (3) for some $\mathsf{m}>0$ and $\{\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)\}_{i=1}^{N}.$ Then,

$$ \lim_{t\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=0\,. $$

Moreover, for $\mathsf{m}^{*}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}(\min_{i}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\max_{i\neq j}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle),$

$$ \inf_{b}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{U_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=e^{-t\mathsf{m}^{*}+o(t)}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem A.3.

The key step in the proof is that the loss can be equivalently re-written as

$$ \begin{split}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};t)&=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle)}{\sum_{j}\exp(t\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle)}\\
&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\Big(1+\sum_{j\neq i}\exp\big(t(\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle\big)\Big).\end{split} $$

Hence, if $\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{U^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{V^{(s)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N};t^{(s)})=0$ indeed holds, then

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}\log\Big(1+\sum_{j\neq i}\exp\big(t^{(s)}(\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle\big)\Big)=0\;\qquad\forall i. $$

Equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{s\longrightarrow+\infty}t^{(s)}\big(\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle\big)=-\infty\;\qquad\forall i\neq j. $$

As all $U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}$ are unit vectors, $\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle\leq 1,\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle\geq-1$ holds for any $i,j,s.$ Hence, for all large enough $s,$

$$ -2\leq\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle\leq 2. $$

In particular, since $t^{(s)}>0,$ Eq. 25 implies that $t^{(s)}\longrightarrow+\infty$ as $s\longrightarrow+\infty$ and

$$ \displaystyle\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{j}^{(s)}\rangle-\langle U_{i}^{(s)},V_{i}^{(s)}\rangle<0\text{ for all $i,j$ and large enough }s. $$

Now, observe that $\{U_{1}^{(s)},U_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,U_{N}^{(s)},V_{1}^{(s)},V_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,V_{N}^{(s)}\}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{\otimes 2N}.$ As $(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{\otimes 2N}$ is a compact set, $\{U_{1}^{(s)},U_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,U_{N}^{(s)},V_{1}^{(s)},V_{2}^{(s)},\ldots,V_{N}^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^{+\infty}$ has a convergent subsequence. Suppose that it converges to $\{U_{1},U_{2},\ldots,U_{N},V_{1},V_{2},\ldots\}.$ By (26) and setting

$$ \mathsf{m}=\min\big(\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\big)/2, $$

we conclude. ∎

### A.4 Triplet Loss

In the context of synchronizing embeddings, the triplet loss function [60] with hyperparameter margin $\alpha$ takes form

$$ \begin{split}&\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Triplet}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};\alpha)=\sum_{i\neq j}\max(\|U_{i}-V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|U_{i}-V_{j}\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha,0).\end{split} $$

#### Observation 4.

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ is a $(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})$ -Constellation. Then, for any $\alpha\leq 4\mathsf{m},$ it is also the case that

$$ \mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Triplet}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};\alpha)=0. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ is a $(\mathsf{m},\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})$ -Constellation. Then, for any $i,\neq j,$ we have that

$$ \displaystyle\|U_{i}-V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|U_{i}-V_{j}\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=2-2\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-(2-2\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle) \displaystyle=2(\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle) \displaystyle\leq 2(-\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}-\mathsf{m}-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})=-4\mathsf{m}. $$

This finishes the proof. ∎

#### Observation 5.

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ is a global minimizer of the one-sided InfoNCE loss with margin $m$ as in Eq. 3 or the regular InfoNCE as in Eq. 22. Then, also for any $\alpha\leq 2m,$

$$ \mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Triplet}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};\alpha)=0. $$

#### Proof.

Note that for any $i\neq j,$

$$ \displaystyle\|U_{i}-V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|U_{i}-V_{j}\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha=\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+\alpha \displaystyle\leq(\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)-m)-(\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)+m)+\alpha=\alpha-2m\leq 0. $$

∎

#### Observation 6.

Suppose that $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ is a global minimizer of the triplet loss for some $\alpha>0.$ Then, also for any $m\leq\alpha/2$ and appropriate $\{\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)\}_{i=}^{N},$ $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ satisfy Eq. 3 and hence

$$ \lim_{t\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{U-InfoNCE}}(\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N};t)=0. $$

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ \|U_{i}-V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-\|U_{i}-V_{j}\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha=2(\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+\alpha/2). $$

Hence, if $\mathcal{L}^{\mathsf{Triplet}}=0,$ for any $i\neq j,$

$$ \langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle+\alpha/2\leq 0. $$

Defining

$$ \begin{split}&\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}(i)=\min_{j}\big(\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle-\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle\big),\\
&m=\alpha/2,\end{split} $$

we reach the conclusion. ∎

Note that while global minimizers of InfoNCE and triplet loss coincide, the global minimizers of sigmoid loss are only a subset of these configurations. This is clearly illustrated by Fig. 2.

## Appendix B Proof of Theorem 3.5: Dimension vs Size tradeoff

#### Proof of Theorem 3.5.

Let

$$ H\sim\mathrm{Unif}(S^{d-1}),\qquad C(H)=\{\,i:\langle c_{i},H\rangle>\delta\},\quad N^{\prime}=|C(H)|, $$

where $c_{i}=(U_{i}+V_{i})/2$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$ will be chosen later.

$$ \|c_{i}\|^{2}=\frac{1+\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle}{2}\in\Bigl[\tfrac{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}{2},1\Bigr],\text{ so }\|c_{i}\|\geq\sqrt{(1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})/2} $$

Then the inner product satisfies

$$ \Pr\bigl[\langle c_{i},H\rangle>\delta\bigr]=\Gamma_{d}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\delta}{\|c_{i}\|}\Bigr)\;\geq\;\Gamma_{d}\!\Bigl(\delta\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}}\Bigr), $$

where $\Gamma_{d}(x)=\Pr[H_{1}>x]$ is strictly decreasing in $x$ . By linearity of expectation,

$$ \mathbb{E}[N^{\prime}]\;\geq\;N\,\Gamma_{d}\!\Bigl(\delta\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}}\Bigr), $$

so there exists a realization of $H$ with

$$ N^{\prime}\;\geq\;N\,\Gamma_{d}\!\Bigl(\delta\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}}\Bigr). $$

Define for the index set $C=C(H)$ the sums

$$ U_{C}=\sum_{i\in C}U_{i},\quad V_{C}=\sum_{i\in C}V_{i},\quad x_{i}=U_{i}-V_{i},\quad x_{C}=\sum_{i\in C}x_{i}, $$

and set

$$ A_{C}=\sum_{i\in C}\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle,\quad B_{C}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in C\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle,\quad\xi_{C}=\frac{1}{N^{\prime}}\Bigl(\sum_{i\in C}\|x_{i}\|^{2}\Bigr)-\|\frac{1}{N^{\prime}}x_{C}\|^{2}\geq 0. $$

A direct expansion shows

$$ \|U_{C}+V_{C}\|^{2}=N^{\prime 2}(2-\xi_{C})\;-\;2(N^{\prime}-2)\,A_{C}\;+\;4\,B_{C}. $$

On the other hand,

$$ \Bigl\|\sum_{i\in C}c_{i}\Bigr\|\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\|U_{C}+V_{C}\|\;\geq\;\sum_{i\in C}\langle c_{i},H\rangle\;>\;N^{\prime}\,\delta, $$

so

$$ \|U_{C}+V_{C}\|^{2}>4N^{\prime 2}\delta^{2}. $$

Combining (29) and (30), and using $A_{C}\geq(\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})N^{\prime}$ and $B_{C}\leq(\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}-\mathsf{m})N^{\prime}(N^{\prime}-1)$ , yields

$$ 4N^{\prime 2}\delta^{2}\;\leq\;N^{\prime 2}(2-\xi_{C})\;-2(N^{\prime}-2)\,(\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})N^{\prime}\;+4\bigl[(\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}-\mathsf{m})\,N^{\prime}(N^{\prime}-1)\bigr] $$

Which means $N^{\prime}\bigl(3\mathsf{m}-1+2\delta^{2}-\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}\bigr)\;\leq\;4\mathsf{m}.$ Where in the last reduction we dropped the $\xi_{C}\geq 0$ term. Hence, whenever $2\delta^{2}>1-3\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}$ ,

$$ N^{\prime}\;\leq\;\frac{4\mathsf{m}}{2\delta^{2}-(1-3\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})}. $$

Combine (28) and (31) to get

$$ N\;\leq\;\frac{4\mathsf{m}}{2\delta^{2}-(1-3\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})}\;\Gamma_{d}\!\Bigl(\delta\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}}\Bigr)^{-1}. $$

Recalling Shannon’s asymptotic lower-bound $\Gamma_{d}(\cos\theta)=\exp\{d\log\sin\theta+o_{\theta}(d)\}$ [62, (11)] with $\cos\theta=\delta\sqrt{2/(1+m+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}})}$ and correponding $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\cos^{2}\theta}=\sqrt{1-\frac{1-3\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}{1+\mathsf{m}+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}},$ the bound is optimized by choosing $\delta=\sqrt{\tfrac{1-3m+\mathsf{b}_{\mathsf{rel}}}{2}}$ . This results in the claimed bound

$$ \;N\leq\exp(-d\log\sin\theta+o_{\theta}(d)).\qed $$

## Appendix C Omitted Proofs from Section 3.3: Combinatorics of The Modality Gap

Here, we analyze configurations $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{\times N}$ with the following property:

$$ \begin{split}&\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle>0\;\forall i,\\
&\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle<0\;\forall i\neq j.\\
\end{split} $$

Ultimately, we aim to prove Theorem 3.6. We also prove several other facts on the way. Our proofs are based on simple facts from convex geometry which we introduce now. One can find more, for example, in the excellent book [3].

### C.1 Preliminaries from Convex Geometry

A set $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is called convex if for any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and any $p,q\in K,$ it is also the case that $\alpha p+(1-\alpha)q\in K.$ In particular, for any points $p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},$ the following two sets are convex. The convex hull defined by

$$ \mathsf{conv}(p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n})\coloneqq\Big\{\alpha_{1}p_{1},\alpha_{2}p_{2}+\cdots+\alpha_{k}p_{k}\;:\;\alpha_{i}\geq 0\qquad\forall i\text{ and }\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}=1\Big\} $$

and the convex cone defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{cone}(p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n})\coloneqq\Big\{\alpha_{1}p_{1},\alpha_{2}p_{2}+\cdots+\alpha_{k}p_{k}\;:\;\alpha_{i}\geq 0\qquad\forall i\text{ and }\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\leq 1\Big\} \displaystyle=\mathsf{conv}(p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n},0). $$

We also introduce the dual cone. For a set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n},$ the dual cone is given by

$$ \mathsf{dualcone}(S)\coloneqq\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;:\;\langle v,x\rangle\geq 0\quad\forall x\in S\}. $$

We will use the following classic theorems from convex geometry.

#### Theorem C.1 (Helly [26]).

Let $X_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n}$ be a finite collection of convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . If the intersection of every $d+1$ of these sets is nonempty, then the intersection of all the sets is nonempty. Formally,

$$ \text{If }\bigcap_{i\in I}X_{i}\neq\emptyset\quad\text{for all }I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}\text{ with }|I|=d+1,\text{then }\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\neq\emptyset. $$

#### Theorem C.2 (Carathéodory [5, 66]).

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . If $\mathbf{x}\in\text{conv}(A)$ , then there exists a set $B\subseteq A$ such that $|B|\leq d+1$ and $\mathbf{x}\in\mathsf{conv}(B)$ .

#### Theorem C.3 (Hyperplane Separation Theorem [48]).

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two nonempty, disjoint convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Then there exists a nonzero vector ${a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a scalar $b$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\langle{a},{x}\rangle\leq b\quad\text{for all }{x}\in X, \displaystyle\langle{a},{y}\rangle\geq b\quad\text{for all }{y}\in Y. $$

### C.2 Combinatorics of Modality Gap

#### Proposition 2.

If (32) hold and $N\geq d+2,$ then there exists some $h\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ such that $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle>0$ for all $i.$

#### Proof.

For each $i=1,\dots,N$ , define the open half-space

$$ H_{i}=\{\,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\ \langle U_{i},x\rangle>0\}. $$

Each $H_{i}$ is convex. We first show that any subcollection of $d+1$ of these half-spaces has nonempty intersection. Indeed, pick distinct indices $i_{1},\dots,i_{d+1}$ ; since $N\geq d+2$ , there is an index $j\notin\{i_{1},\dots,i_{d+1}\}$ . By (32), for each $k=1,\dots,d+1$ ,

$$ \langle U_{i_{k}},V_{j}\rangle<0\text{ , so }\bigl\langle U_{i_{k}},-V_{j}\bigr\rangle>0, $$

and $-V_{j}\in\bigcap_{k=1}^{d+1}H_{i_{k}}\neq\varnothing$ .

Since every $d+1$ of the $H_{i}$ intersect and $N\geq d+2$ , Helly’s theorem implies

$$ \bigcap_{i=1}^{N}H_{i}\;\neq\;\varnothing. $$

Choose any $h_{0}\in\bigcap_{i=1}^{N}H_{i}$ . Then $\langle h_{0},U_{i}\rangle>0$ for all $i$ . Setting $h=h_{0}/\|h_{0}\|\in\mathbb{S}$ preserves these strict inequalities. ∎

#### Proposition 3.

If (32) hold and $N\geq d+2,$ then there exists some $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ such that $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle>0$ for all $i$ and $h\in\mathsf{conv}(U_{1},U_{2},\ldots,U_{N}).$

#### Proof.

Let $C:=\operatorname{conv}(U_{1},\dots,U_{N})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , a compact convex set. Take the unit vector $h$ given by Proposition 2 and denote by $h^{\prime}$ its projection onto $C$ . This implies the fact that that the hyperplane

$$ H:=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle h-h^{\prime},\,x-h^{\prime}\rangle=0\bigr\} $$

supports the set $C$ at the point $h^{\prime}$ : all points of $C$ (hence each $U_{i}$ ) lie in the closed half-space

$$ H^{-}:=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle h-h^{\prime},\,x-h^{\prime}\rangle\leq 0\bigr\}, $$

whereas $h$ itself belongs to the opposite open half-space $H^{+}:=\{x:\langle h-h^{\prime},x-h^{\prime}\rangle>0\}$ . Choose an orthonormal basis $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{d}\}$ with

$$ e_{1}:=\frac{h-h^{\prime}}{\|h-h^{\prime}\|}. $$

In these coordinates

$$ h=h^{\prime}+\alpha e_{1},\quad\alpha:=\|h-h^{\prime}\|>0,\qquad h^{\prime}=0\cdot e_{1}+h^{\prime}_{\perp}, $$

while every $U_{i}$ has a decomposition $U_{i}=U_{i,1}\,e_{1}+U_{i,\perp}$ with $U_{i,1}\leq 0$ .

For each $i$ ,

$$ \langle h^{\prime},U_{i}\rangle-\langle h,U_{i}\rangle=\langle h^{\prime}-h,\,U_{i}\rangle=-\alpha\,U_{i,1}\;\geq\;0. $$

Because $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle>0$ , we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\langle h^{\prime},U_{i}\rangle>0\qquad(i=1,\dots,N). $$

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.6.

Let $h$ be the vector provided by Proposition 3, so $h\in\operatorname{conv}(U_{1},\dots,U_{N})$ and $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle>0$ for every $i$ . Set the cone

$$ C^{\prime}:=\operatorname{cone}\{U_{1},\dots,U_{N}\}=\Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}U_{i}\,:\,a_{i}\geq 0\Bigr\}. $$

Because each $U_{i}$ has positive dot product with $h$ , define the affine hyperplane

$$ H:=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle x,h\rangle=1\bigr\}. $$

Every ray $\{\lambda U_{i}:\lambda>0\}$ meets $H$ once, namely at

$$ Q_{i}:=\frac{1}{\langle U_{i},h\rangle}\,U_{i}\;\in H. $$

Consequently

$$ C^{\prime}\cap H\;=\;\operatorname{conv}\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{N}\}. $$

The the vector $h^{\dagger}$ in $H$ which is parallel to $h$ . $\langle h^{\dagger},h\rangle=1$ , so $h^{\dagger}$ is $h$ rescaled by a positive scalar. Since $h^{\dagger}$ also lies in $\operatorname{conv}(U_{1},\dots,U_{N})\subset C^{\prime}$ , we have $h^{\dagger}\in C^{\prime}\cap H$ . The hyperplane $H$ is $(d-1)$ –dimensional. By Carathéodory’s theorem in $\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$ , there is a subset $S\subset\{1,\dots,N\}$ with $|S|\leq d$ and weights $\lambda_{i}\geq 0$ , $\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}=1$ , such that

$$ h^{\dagger}\;=\;\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}\,Q_{i}\;=\;\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}\,\frac{U_{i}}{\langle U_{i},h\rangle}. $$

Fix $k\notin S$ . Using Theorem C.2 and (32),

$$ \langle h^{\dagger},V_{k}\rangle=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}\,\frac{\langle U_{i},V_{k}\rangle}{\langle U_{i},h\rangle}<0, $$

because each numerator $\langle U_{i},V_{k}\rangle$ is negative and each denominator $\langle U_{i},h\rangle$ is positive. Hence $\langle h^{\dagger},V_{k}\rangle<0$ for every $k\notin S$ . Only the (at most) $d$ indices in $S$ may give a non–negative value. Note that $h^{\dagger}$ is already on the unit circle. ∎

Now we prove that there is a construction for which this bound is almost tight and we can separate all but at least $d-1$ vectors with a hyperplane.

#### Construction 3 (Tightness of Theorem 3.6).

There exists a set of vectors $\{(U_{i},V_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ such that $\langle U_{i},V_{i}\rangle>0$ for each $i,$ $\langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle<0$ for each $i\neq j,$ and for any $h\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},$ at least for $d-1$ values of $i,$ it holds that $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle$ and $\langle h,V_{i}\rangle$ have the same sign.

#### Proof.

For the construction for $d=3$ , note that we can take two parallel $k$ -gons equally far from the equator of the sphere such that the zeniths of their points for one of them is $\pi/4+\delta$ and for the other one is $3/4\pi-\delta$ and by taking $\delta\to 0$ we can ensure that the dot product between corresponding pairs is positive and the dot product between non-matching pairs is negative. Now note that by taking $k$ sufficiently large and the $\delta$ sufficiently small. The intersection of that configuration with the wedge with dihedral angle $\alpha$ contains at least $N-2$ points from one of the $k$ -gons (the $U$ ’s) and $N-2$ points from the other (the $V$ ’s) for any value of $\alpha$ . See Fig. 14.

*Figure 14: Construction in 3D.*

Label those as

$$ U_{1},\dots,U_{N-2}\quad\text{and}\quad V_{1},\dots,V_{N-2}. $$

Finally place two more pairs on the equator:

$$ U_{N-1}=V_{N-1},\quad U_{N}=V_{N} $$

chosen so that $\langle U_{N-1},U_{N}\rangle<0$ and both make negative dot-products with each wedge boundary ray. This completes the $d=3$ example.

For the general case ( $d>3$ ). Let $\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{d+1}$ be the vertices of a regular simplex in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Set

$$ U_{i}=V_{i}=\omega_{i},\quad i=1,\dots,d-3. $$

These occupy a $(d-3)$ –dimensional subspace. In the orthogonal complement (which is 3–dimensional), embed the $d=3$ construction, obtaining pairs $(U_{d-2},V_{d-2}),\dots,(U_{N},V_{N})$ . Finally, pick a small $\varepsilon>0$ and renormalize:

$$ U_{i}^{\prime}=\varepsilon\,\omega_{d-2}\;+\;\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}\;U_{i},\quad V_{i}^{\prime}=\varepsilon\,\omega_{d-2}\;+\;\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}\;V_{i},\quad i=d-2,\dots,N. $$

For $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, all the required dot-product signs are preserved, and since the configuration was orthogonal to $U_{i}$ for $i=1,2,\dots,d-3$ ,

$$ \langle U_{i},V_{j}\rangle=-\epsilon\frac{1}{d}<0,\forall i=1,2,\dots,d-3,j=d-2,d-1,\dots,N, $$

as needed. ∎

#### Proposition 4.

If (32) hold then $U_{i}\not\in\mathsf{cone}(\{U_{j}\}_{j\neq i})$ for any $i.$

#### Proof.

Suppose, to the contrary, that for some fixed $i$ there exist scalars $a_{j}\geq 0$ for $j\neq i$ such that

$$ U_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j\neq i}a_{j}\,U_{j}. $$

Taking the inner product with $V_{i}$ gives

$$ \langle V_{i},U_{i}\rangle\;=\;\sum_{j\neq i}a_{j}\,\langle V_{i},U_{j}\rangle. $$

Since by (32) we have $\langle V_{i},U_{j}\rangle<0$ for all $j\neq i$ and each $a_{j}\geq 0$ , the right–hand side is nonpositive. But the left–hand side is strictly positive, a contradiction. Therefore $U_{i}\notin\mathsf{cone}(\{U_{j}\}_{j\neq i})$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.

If $d=2$ and $N\geq 4,$ there does not exist a configuration satisfying (32).

#### Proof.

Because $N\geq d+2$ , Proposition 3 gives a unit vector $h$ with $\langle h,U_{i}\rangle>0$ for every $i$ . Rotate so $h=(1,0)$ ; all $U_{i}$ now lie in the open right half-plane $x>0$ . Write their polar angles in $(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ as

$$ -\tfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<\dots<\theta_{N}<\tfrac{\pi}{2}. $$

Now note that $U_{2}\in\mathsf{cone}(U_{1},U_{3})$ which is a contradiction by Proposition 4. Therefore configuration (32) cannot exist when $d=2$ and $N\geq 4$ . ∎

## Appendix E Connection to Linear Representation Hypothesis Across Modalities

It has been observed by many authors that modern dense embedding spaces acquire correspondence between linear-algebraic operations and real-world concepts. This has been immortalized as “King - Man + Woman $\approx$ Queen” in word2vec [47] and is also observed in modern LLMs as well [52, 68]. Curiously, we find that contrastive pretraining with sigmoid loss also leads to a special case of LRH: there emerges a direction $\bar{x}$ such that adding it to an image embedding (almost) recovers the embedding of a matching text caption. Indeed, looking at the optimal embeddings in Fig. 6 we can see that $U_{i}-V_{i}$ does not depend on $i$ , which we take as a manifestation of LRH in this context (the concept being “shift text to image” or more generally one modality to another). Furthermore, both our upper and lower bounds on the cardinality of the embeddings in Section 3.2 require Cross-Modality-LRH satisfying configurations to be tight.

In the proof of Theorem 3.5 in Appendix B we defined the following quantity characterizing an arbitrary constellation

$$ \xi=\frac{1}{N}\Bigl(\sum_{i}\|x_{i}\|^{2}\Bigr)-\|\bar{x}\|^{2}\geq 0\,, $$

where $x_{i}=U_{i}-V_{i}$ and $\bar{x}={1\over N}\sum_{i}x_{i}$ . (In the proof $\xi$ was defined for a carefully chosen sub-constellation). We note that the upper bound in that Theorem 3.5 could only possibly be tight if $\xi\approx 0$ . In this section we will further show that $\xi$ can be used as a quantitative measure of the degree to which Linear Representation Hypothesis is satisfied.

First, let us establish that when $\xi$ is small (as $\xi\geq 0$ is used in the proof of Theorem 3.5 this means that the bounds in that proof are tight). More importantly, a small $\xi$ implies something significant about our representations: it suggests that the difference vector, $U_{i}-V_{i}$ , is nearly identical for all indices $i$ . Think of it this way: if you have two sets of learned representations, say $U_{i}$ for images and $V_{i}$ for their corresponding text descriptions, a small $\xi$ means that you can apply a consistent shift (a single vector) to all the $V_{i}$ vectors to transform them into their corresponding $U_{i}$ vectors. So, by shifting a text representation, you could get its corresponding image representation.

#### Proposition 6.

If $\xi=o(1)$ then $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|x_{i}-\bar{x}\|^{2}=o(1)$ and all pairs of representations align in the sense that $U_{i}-V_{i}\approx U_{j}-V_{j}$ for all $i,j$ . In particular, the $U$ ’s are obtained from the $V$ ’s by adding a vector $\bar{x}$ , which thus serves as a concept shift.

#### Proof.

A simple algebra shows that $\xi$ has the following two equivalent expressions:

$$ \xi=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|x_{i}-\bar{x}\|^{2}={1\over 2N^{2}}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|^{2}\,. $$

Thus, the statement " $\xi=o(1)$ " is equivalent to

$$ 0\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|x_{i}-\bar{x}\|^{2}\to 0\,, $$

which in turn implies that $U_{i}-V_{i}\approx\bar{x}$ simultaneously for all $i$ . The argument for $U_{i}-V_{i}\approx U_{j}-V_{j}$ is similar. ∎

#### Corollary 2.

If $\xi=0$ , then $U_{i}-V_{i}$ are all identical for all indices $i$ .

Indeed, in Fig. 21 when training directly the representations, we can observe the $\xi$ value converging to 0 for a range of different dimensions.
